cards.front: Defend to the Aufsichtsrat in three sentences: why does the Problemfall use 95% rather than 99.9%, and what is the consequence for capital?

rubric.text: Problemfall is the ~1-in-20-year (95%) view; Extremfall is the ~1-in-1000-year (99.9%) economic-capital view
Only the quantile Φ⁻¹(q) changes inside the conditional PD — nothing else
The Problemfall UL is therefore far smaller (≈¼ here: 15,520 vs 67,400)

antiPoints: claims LGD or the 0.71/1.33 scalar changes between the scenarios
double-counts EL in the capital figure
cards.modelAnswer: The Problemfall measures risk-bearing capacity at a 95% confidence (a loss exceeded about once in 20 years), reserved for the going-concern traffic-light view, whereas the Extremfall uses 99.9% as a liquidation/economic-capital lens. Mechanically only the quantile Φ⁻¹(q) is swapped (1.6449 vs 3.0902) inside the conditional-PD term — LGD, R(PD) and the maturity adjustment are unchanged. The result is a materially smaller unexpected loss (here roughly a quarter: €15,520 vs €67,400).

cards.front: An examiner asks: the IRB formula already covers credit risk — why does the Leitfaden add an HHI granularity surcharge?

rubric.text: ASRF assumes an infinitely granular portfolio, so single-name concentration is invisible to the formula
Real corporate books are lumpy, so a surcharge UL·HHI captures the extra unexpected loss

antiPoints: claims the surcharge adds expected loss
confuses it with the maturity adjustment
cards.modelAnswer: The ASRF model that underlies the IRB formula assumes an infinitely granular portfolio, so by construction it ignores single-name (and sector) concentration. Real corporate books are lumpy, so the Leitfaden bolts on a granularity surcharge UL·HHI to capture the unexpected loss the formula structurally cannot see; the new UL is UL·(1+HHI).
